Diagonals of rational power series and their uses in combinatorics, number theory, and computer science

Jason Bell (University of Waterloo)

Given a power series \( F(x_1, \ldots, x_d) = \text{lsum } f_{-}(i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_d) \times 1^A(i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_d) \), one can form a one-variable power series \(\text{lDelta}(F)(t) = \text{lsum } f_{-}(n, n, \ldots, n)\) t\(^A\)n, called the diagonal of \(F\). When \(F\) is the power series expansion of a rational function, the diagonal enjoys of \(F\) enjoys many nice properties, including satisfying a linear homogeneous differential equation with polynomial coefficients. Many natural generating functions arising in combinatorial enumeration can be expressed as diagonals and this fact often gives one a wealth of information about congruences of coefficients mod primes and asymptotic information. We give a survey of the theory of diagonals and discuss some more recent results and some of their applications to other areas of mathematics.

Given a sequence whose generating function is the diagonal of a rational power series, we provide a method, based on work of J. Denef and L. Lipshitz [J. Number Theory 26, 46–67 (1987; Zbl 0609.12020)], for computing a finite automaton for the sequence modulo \(p^\alpha\), for all but finitely many primes \(p\). This method gives completely automatic proofs of known results, establishes a number of new theorems for well-known sequences, and allows us to resolve some conjectures regarding the Apéry numbers. We also give a second method, which applies to an algebraic sequence modulo \(p^\alpha\) for all primes \(p\), but is significantly slower. Finally, we show that a broad range of multidimensional sequences possess Lucas products modulo \(p\).

In the past decade, many researchers have been interested in congruences for various algebraic sequences modulo prime powers. Deutsch and Sagan [DS06] studied arithmetic properties of several sequences, including the Catalan and Motzkin numbers. They posited conjectures regarding Motzkin numbers modulo 4 and 8, which were proved by Eu, Liu, and Yeh [ELY08]. Congruences for Catalan numbers have also been studied by Liu and Yeh [LY10], Xin and Xu [XX11], and Lin [Lin12]. The techniques used to prove these results depend to some extent on the particular sequences considered, and in some cases the proofs occupy entire papers. Kauers, Krattenthaler, and Müller developed the first systematic methods for producing congruences modulo \(2^{\alpha}\) in [KKM12] and modulo \(3^{\alpha}\) in [KM13] for a large family of differentially algebraic sequences, including many algebraic sequences. As examples they produce automatic proofs of many existing results.  

In this paper we show how to discover and prove congruences for algebraic sequences over \(\mathbb{Q}(x)\) in a general fashion — for any algebraic sequence modulo any prime power. A natural setting for these results is that of automatic sequences. A \(p\) - automatic sequence is a sequence \((a_{n})_{n \geq 0}\) on a finite alphabet, where \(a_{n}\) is the output of a finite- state automaton when fed the standard base- \(p\) representation of \(n\) . We postpone the formal definition until Section 1.2. The following result provides a fundamental link between automaticity and algebraicity; let \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\) denote the finite field of size \(p\) .  

Theorem 1.1 (Christol et al. [CKMF80]). Let \((a_{n})_{n \geq 0}\) be a sequence of elements in \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\) . Then \(\sum_{n \geq 0} a_{n} x^{n}\) is algebraic over \(\mathbb{F}_{p}(x)\) if and only if \((a_{n})_{n \geq 0}\) is \(p\) - automatic.  

A proof also appears in [AS03, Theorem 12.2.5]. It follows immediately that if \((a_{n})_{n \geq 0}\) is an algebraic sequence of integers (or, more generally, \(p\) - adic integers), then \((a_{n} \bmod p)_{n \geq 0}\) is \(p\) - automatic, since projecting modulo \(p\) a polynomial for which \(\sum_{n \geq 0} a_{n} x^{n}\) is a root yields a polynomial for which \(\sum_{n \geq 0} (a_{n} \bmod p) x^{n}\) is a root.  

The proof of Theorem 1.1 is constructive in the sense that, given a polynomial for which \(\sum_{n \geq 0} a_{n} x^{n}\) is a root, there is an algorithm for producing an automaton that computes \(a_{n} \bmod p\) . # Title: Automatic congruences for diagonals of rational functions

(Submitted on 31 Oct 2013 (v1), last revised 23 Apr 2014 (this version, v2))

Abstract: In this paper we use the framework of automatic sequences to study
combinatorial sequences modulo prime powers. Given a sequence whose generating
function is the diagonal of a rational power series, we provide a method, based
on work of Denef and Lipshitz, for computing a finite automaton for the
sequence modulo $p^\alpha$, for all but finitely many primes $p$. This method
gives completely automatic proofs of known results, establishes a number of new
theorems for well-known sequences, and allows us to resolve some conjectures
regarding the Ap\'ery numbers. We also give a second method, which applies to
an algebraic sequence modulo $p^\alpha$ for all primes $p$, but is
significantly slower. Finally, we show that a broad range of multidimensional
sequences possess Lucas products modulo $p$.

## 1 Introduction  

Given an algebraic function \(\eta\) over \(\mathbb{C}(x)\) , Abel's problem, as mentioned by Boulanger in [8, p. 93], consists in determining if the differential equation  

\[y^{\prime} = \eta y \quad (1.1)\]  

admits a non- trivial solution \(y\) algebraic over \(\mathbb{C}(x)\) . This problem naturally occurs in procedures to decide in a finite number of steps if all solutions of a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients are algebraic over \(\mathbb{C}(x)\) , see [2, 29]. A decision procedure to solve Abel's problem was first given by Risch [26] and later independently by Baldassarri and Dwork [2, Section 6].  

In this paper, we are interested in the restriction of Abel's problem to the functions \(\eta\) algebraic over \(\mathbb{C}(x)\) that admit a Puiseux expansion with rational coefficients at some point \(\delta\) in \(\mathbb{C}\cup \{\infty \}\) .

Obviously the above mentioned decision procedures also apply in this context but we present here an arithmetic criterion based on Gauss congruences for \(x\eta (x)\) that proves effective in applications. It is stated as Theorem 1 in Section 1.1, where we use in particular a consequence of Grothendieck's conjecture proved in rank one by Chudnovsky and Chudnovsky [11].

Diagonals of rational power series and their uses in combinatorics, number theory, and computer science

Jason Bell (University of Waterloo)

Given a power series \( F(x_1, \ldots, x_d) = \text{lsum } f_{-}(i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_d) \times 1^A(i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_d) \), one can form a one-variable power series \(\text{lDelta}(F)(t) = \text{lsum } f_{-}(n, n, \ldots, n)\) t\(^A\)n, called the diagonal of \(F\). When \(F\) is the power series expansion of a rational function, the diagonal enjoys of \(F\) enjoys many nice properties, including satisfying a linear homogeneous differential equation with polynomial coefficients. Many natural generating functions arising in combinatorial enumeration can be expressed as diagonals and this fact often gives one a wealth of information about congruences of coefficients mod primes and asymptotic information. We give a survey of the theory of diagonals and discuss some more recent results and some of their applications to other areas of mathematics.

It soon became apparent that this vanishing coefficient phenomenon occurred only for primes \(p\equiv 1\) (mod 4). Further investigation revealed that it occurred for pairs of exponents \((j,k)\) of the form \((j,k) = (b m,b n)\) , where \(p = m^{2} + n^{2}\) and \(b\in \mathbb{N}\) . These investigations suggested that in this situation, \(a_{p t + c b^{2} + d b}^{(b m,b n)} = 0\) for all integers \(t\) and some pair of integers \(c\) and \(d\) and also allowed us to guess formulae for \(c\) and \(d\) . In particular, for \(p\equiv 1\) (mod 12) one pair was \((c,d) = (0,w)\) , where \(w = \bar{2} (m + n)\) (mod \(p\) ).  

One method of proof that occurred to us was the "involution" described above at (1.13)- (1.17). For example, for a given prime \(p\equiv 1\) (mod 12) one finds \(m\) and \(n\) such that \(p = m^{2} + n^{2}\) and \(3\mid m\) and selects one of the \(\tau\) found experimentally, such as \(\tau = w\coloneqq \bar{2} (m + n)\) . Then using a computer algebra system such as Mathematica one follows through the steps described in the introduction as far as computing \(g(\mathbf{x})\) as described at (1.11).  

Next, one sets up a matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) with entries \(a_{i,j}\) to be determined, and likewise a vector \(\mathbf{b}\) with entries \(b_{k}\) to be determined. One computes \(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\coloneqq \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}\) as at (1.13) and then the difference \(g(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}) - g(\mathbf{x})\) , which we wish to be identically zero. Regarded as a polynomial in \(r\) , \(s\) , \(u\) and \(v\) , setting the coefficients of this polynomial equal to zero gives a system of fifteen quadratic equations in the \(a_{i,j}\) and \(b_{k}\) for which we seek integral solutions.  

Each of these equations may have, in some cases, hundreds or even thousands of solutions, so attempting to solve all fifteen equations simultaneously with a single Solve[] command is not practical, time- wise. In [69], Mimura also studied the Apéry numbers more extensively, and deduced many congruence properties for them. Extending certain results of Mimura, Beukers [16] proved the following supercongruences for the Apéry numbers.  

Theorem 1.2.1 ([16], Theorem 1). Let \(m, r \in \mathbb{N}\) and \(p > 3\) . Then  

\[A_{m p^{r} - 1} \equiv A_{m p^{r - 1} - 1} \pmod{p^{3r}} \quad (1.2.2)\]  

\[B_{m p^{r} - 1} \equiv B_{m p^{r - 1} - 1} \pmod{p^{3r}}. \quad (1.2.3)\]  

Beukers [18] further conjectured some divisibility conditions for the Apéry numbers, which are recently confirmed by Delaygue [24] in a general set up.  

The development of the Apéry numbers and their related congruences motivated mathematicians to introduce mathematically riched other number theoretical objects exhibiting similar types of properties. In [23], Coster considered a generalization of the Apéry numbers given by the formula  

\[A(n,m,\ell ,\lambda)\coloneqq \sum_{k = 0}^{n}{\binom{n}{k}}^{m}{\binom{n + k}{k}}^{\ell}\lambda^{k}.\]  

Generalizing the congruences (1.2.1), (1.2.2), and (1.2.3) on Apéry numbers, Coster proved that, for \(m, \ell \in \mathbb{N}, \lambda = \pm 1\) and \(p \geq 5\) ,  

\[\begin{array}{c}{A(s p^{r},m,\ell ,\lambda)\equiv A(s p^{r - 1},m,\ell ,\lambda)\pmod{p^{3r}}\mathrm{if}m\geq 3,}\\ {A(s p^{r} - 1,m,\ell ,\lambda)\equiv A(s p^{r - 1} - 1,m,\ell ,\lambda)\pmod{p^{3r}}\mathrm{if}\ell \geq 3.} \end{array} \quad (1.2.4)\]  

Deutsch and Sagan [25] showed that the generalized Apéry numbers \(A(n, m, \ell, 1)\) also follow the Lucas congruence modulo an odd prime \(p\) , and characterized their congruence classes modulo 3 in terms of precise conditions which the 3- adic expansion of \(n\) must satisfy. It has been noticed that the Apery numbers can be represented as diagonal coefficients of certain rational functions, and the diagonal coefficients of a rational function with integral Taylor coefficients are algebraic modulo \(p^{\alpha}\) for any \(\alpha\) . Using this, Straub [89] extended some properties of the Apery numbers to infinite families of sequences of such numbers. \[\beta_{n} = \sum_{j = 0}^{n}{\binom{n}{j}}^{2}{\binom{2(j)}{j}}{\binom{2(n - j)}{n - j}}\]
